Plain, spaced, caps: one, one, three.","headline":{"text":"token = text piece, one integer","semantic":"concept"},"tags":["plain","spaced","capitals"],"statCards":[{"value":"1, 1, 3","label":"tokens: plain, spaced, caps","sourceRef":"num-7"}],"source":"glyphcut README"},{"beatId":"b2","narration":"A tokenizer turns text into tokens the model can number. Cut by character and sequences balloon. Cut by word and the vocabulary, its fixed list of pieces, explodes. So tokenizers learn subword pieces instead.","headline":{"text":"vocabulary = fixed list of output pieces","semantic":"concept"},"tags":["characters","whole words","subwords"]},{"beatId":"b3","narration":"Learning starts from two hundred and fifty-six byte values, so nothing is unknown. It counts every neighbouring pair and adds the most frequent. The pair \"t\" plus \"h\" becomes \"th\", repeated until the vocabulary hits its target.","headline":{"text":"Frequent pairs become new symbols","semantic":"concept"},"tags":["most frequent pair","new symbol"],"statCards":[{"value":"256","label":"byte values to start","sourceRef":"num-2"}],"source":"A field guide to subword merges"},{"beatId":"b4","narration":"Encoding replays merges in the order learned. So \"the\" collapses to one token. A rare word like \"glimmerwick\" stays in several pieces: no merge ever joined those pairs.","headline":{"text":"Common words collapse to one token","semantic":"concept"},"tags":["common word","rare word","merge order"]},{"beatId":"b5","narration":"Here's the catch: before any merge, pre-tokenization splits text into chunks that merges never cross. A leading space sticks to the next word; capitals change the pieces. So \"Paris\" is one token, \" Paris\" one, \"PARIS\" three.","headline":{"text":"pre-tokenization = splitting text into merge-proof chunks","semantic":"concept"},"tags":["pre-tokenization","leading space","capitals"],"source":"glyphcut README"},{"beatId":"b6","narration":"Corrowby billed every request by token and budgeted prompts in words. English replies ran about one point three tokens per word. A language rare in training needed about three times as many, so the estimate failed.","headline":{"text":"A word is not a token","semantic":"problem"},"tags":["billed per token","word estimates"],"statCards":[{"value":"about 1.3","label":"tokens per English word","sourceRef":"num-4"}],"source":"Field notes: counting tokens before you pay for them"},{"beatId":"b7","narration":"Corrowby now counts every reply with the model's own tokenizer, so the Paris line is priced exactly. Guess the tokens and you guess the bill.","headline":{"text":"Exact counts replace word estimates","semantic":"resolution"},"tags":["exact tokenizer","token budgets"]}]}
